titulo.texto: Recreation of Tomb 104 at Monte Albán

frase_gancho.texto: An underground house painted to welcome the ancestors.

puente_narrativo.texto: The Zapotec built it. Centuries later, another people reopened a Zapotec tomb to bury their king with a treasure of gold. Look for a jewel made of several plates, with little bells, that jingled with every step.

guion_corto.texto: You are standing before a full-size reproduction of Tomb 104 at Monte Albán, discovered in 1937 by the archaeologist Alfonso Caso. The Zapotec buried their lords beneath the floors of their house courtyards, in stone chambers that were true underground palaces. On the façade you will see a panel with a molding typical of Monte Albán and, above the door, a niche holding a clay urn. Look inside: the walls copy the original paintings, in red, blue, yellow, and black, where a procession of figures marches toward the back of the tomb wearing feather headdresses, carrying bags of copal and incense burners, alongside glyphs of the calendar.

guion_largo.texto:
In many places, the dead are buried far from the living. The Zapotec did the opposite: they buried important people beneath their own homes, and relatives went down to visit them. A tomb was not a place of forgetting, but the house where the grandfather went on looking after the family. People brought him food, burned incense for him, and spoke with him. The dead were part of daily life.

What you have in front of you is a full-scale reproduction. The real tomb is still at Monte Albán; here it was rebuilt with faithful copies of its paintings so that you can look in as if you were going down the stairs. Let us begin with the façade. The panel that crowns it has a double molding, a frame within a frame, which archaeologists call a “double scapular” and which is a hallmark of Monte Albán architecture. It is like a signature.

Above the door opens a niche that holds a clay urn, like the ones you already know from [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo) and from [Cozobi](mna_s07_urna_cozobi). It is a guardian that watches over the entrance. Specialists do not agree on which divine figure it represents, but they do agree on its function: to protect the dead and connect them with the gods. And inside, in the chamber, more urns were placed, as part of the offering around the deceased.

Now comes the best part: the murals. Look in and notice the side walls. A long line of figures advances in the same direction, toward the back, each one with its feathers and with the objects of the rite in their hands. In front of them are calendar glyphs that look like names and dates. It is thought that these are the ancestors, or priests, who accompany the dead person on the journey and receive them on the other side. The painting is very well preserved, and that is rare: few tombs in Mesoamerica retain murals of this quality.

The tomb was discovered by Alfonso Caso in 1937. Caso worked at Monte Albán for years: in 1932 he had found Tomb 7, whose jewels you will see in a few steps, and in 1937, this one. Between the two he revolutionized what was known about Oaxaca: he showed that Monte Albán had been a great city, much older than the Mexica, and that it had been Zapotec before it was Mixtec.

For the Zapotec, ancestors were intermediaries. It was believed that the dead of important families could ask Cocijo for rain, the gods for abundance, and protection for the city. That is why they had to be honored well: the tomb was a house, but also a kind of window to the sky. And that is why lords were buried close to their people: their dead were their guarantee.

All of this has not disappeared. In Oaxaca, the Day of the Dead is one of the most important celebrations of the year: altars are set up with food, copal, and marigold flowers, the same flower that was offered to [Xochipilli](mna_s06_xochipilli), and the visit of the departed is awaited. When you go up to the halls upstairs, you will see altars of the dead from several peoples: they are the descendants of this custom.

Before moving on, walk toward the entrance and look inside once more: that procession advancing without stopping. Whoever painted it knew that all of us would one day reach the back of the tomb, and wanted the journey to be beautiful.

texto: Find the panel on the façade with its double frame
Look inside and follow the procession of painted figures
Find the bags of copal and the incense burners they carry in their hands

texto.Material: Museum recreation at 1:1 scale of the façade with niche and the funerary chamber painted in fresco, accompanied by original clay urns and vessels
texto.Discovery: Discovered and explored by Alfonso Caso in 1937

texto.pregunta: Myth: Pre-Hispanic tombs were fearful places, sealed and forgotten.
texto.respuesta: Reality: For the Zapotec they were living houses: they were reopened to leave offerings and speak with the ancestors.
